name: Hamstring Strain
summary: Musculotendinous hamstring injury commonly occurring during high-speed running or excessive lengthening.

looksLike: Pain on stretch or resisted contraction
redFlags: Inability to walk normally after severe injury
selfCare: Avoid complete rest once walking is comfortable

assess: Pain/weakness with resisted knee flexion or hip extension
Reduced tolerance to lengthened hamstring position
Possible palpable defect in severe injury

tests.name: Resisted Knee Flexion Test
tests.purpose: Reproduce pain and assess hamstring force.
tests.positive: Concordant posterior-thigh pain and/or meaningful weakness.

tests.name: Passive Straight-Leg Raise / Length Test
tests.purpose: Assess symptom response to hamstring lengthening.
tests.positive: Localized posterior-thigh pain or clearly reduced pain-limited range compared with the other side.

differentials: DVT when swelling/risk factors are concerning

stages.label: Protect & Begin Loading
stages.goal: Settle acute irritability while preventing excessive deconditioning.
dose: Short-length isometric or low-load concentric knee flexion: 3–5 x 20–30 s or 3 x 10–15

stages.label: Strength Through Range
stages.goal: Restore force across progressively longer muscle lengths.

stages.label: Eccentric, Running & Sprinting
stages.goal: Restore high-speed and sport-specific hamstring capacity.
dose: Nordic: begin low volume such as 2 x 4–6 and progress
Running speed progressed in steps with pain-free sprinting as a late criterion
High-speed exposures separated by recovery days

returnCriteria: No significant symptoms after previous loading

logic: Early controlled loading is usually better than long rest.
Long-length strength and gradual sprint exposure are important because recurrence risk is high.
Suspect proximal avulsion when there is sudden severe proximal pain, bruising and major weakness.
structures: Biceps femoris long head commonly in sprint-type injury
Proximal free tendon in some injuries
mechanism: Excessive hip flexion with knee extension
classification: Grade III major/complete tear; proximal avulsion must be excluded
investigations: MRI/ultrasound can help grade severe injury or suspected proximal tendon avulsion.
Imaging is not required for every mild strain.
manual: Gentle soft-tissue techniques can be used for comfort after the acute phase.
Avoid aggressive stretching or deep pressure over a fresh tear.
Manual therapy does not replace progressive loading and sprint re-exposure.
Gentle soft-tissue treatment after acute irritability settles
Do not aggressively massage an acute tear or hematoma
Avoid deep massage over an acute tear or hematoma.
Gentle soft-tissue work can be added later for comfort, but loading is the main treatment.
modalities: Ice/compression may be used for short-term comfort in the acute phase.
Passive modalities have a limited role compared with progressive rehabilitation.
Compression/cold early for comfort if useful
Avoid excessive passive stretching immediately after significant strain
Compression/cold early only for comfort/swelling management.
Do not let passive treatment delay loading progression.
dosing: Running: walk-jog → moderate speed → high speed → sprint.
progression: Increase eccentric load and long-length strength
Progress when walking is pain-free and strength improves.
Increase running speed gradually; do not jump from jogging directly to maximal sprinting.
Include long-length and high-speed preparation before return to sport.
mistakes: Returning when jogging is pain-free but sprint exposure is absent
Aggressive stretching in the acute stage.
Returning when pain is gone but strength remains reduced.
pearls: Late rehab must include high-speed exposure for athletes who sprint.
Progress based on symptoms, strength and response to previous loading—not calendar time alone.
education: Explain recurrence risk and why high-speed preparation matters.
Use soreness next day to adjust training dose.
escalation: Imaging/orthopedic review for suspected avulsion, major defect or unusually poor recovery

tests.name: Resisted Knee Flexion Test
tests.purpose: Reproduce pain and assess hamstring force.
tests.positive: Concordant posterior-thigh pain and/or meaningful weakness.
tests.patientPosition: Prone or sitting with the knee flexed to the chosen test angle.
tests.handPlacement: Stabilize thigh/pelvis as needed; resistance applied at distal leg.
procedure: Ask the patient to flex the knee against resistance.
Test at more than one knee angle when appropriate.
Compare pain and force with the other side.
tests.interpretation: Supports hamstring musculotendinous injury when localized to the injured region.

tests.name: Passive Straight-Leg Raise / Length Test
tests.purpose: Assess symptom response to hamstring lengthening.
tests.positive: Localized posterior-thigh pain or clearly reduced pain-limited range compared with the other side.
tests.handPlacement: Support heel/calf and maintain knee extension.
procedure: Stop at symptom onset or firm end-feel.
Compare side-to-side and note symptom location.
tests.interpretation: Supports length sensitivity; neural symptoms require separate neurodynamic interpretation.

story.headline: The sprinter who was fine at jogging—and not ready to sprint
story.scene: A winger accelerates to chase a ball and feels a sharp snap in the back of the thigh. Weeks later he can jog and proudly announces, 'I'm cured.' His sport, however, has a second gear.
story.dialogue: Player: 'I ran slowly without pain!' Therapist: 'Excellent trailer. We still need to test the action scene.'
story.clue: Sprint-type injury often involves the biceps femoris long head. Grade and location matter, and marked proximal weakness, bruising or a palpable defect may signal avulsion requiring referral.
story.twist: Overstretching a fresh tear can irritate it; never confuse early flexibility with restored high-speed force capacity.
story.aha: Jogging is not the final exam for an athlete whose job is sprinting.
story.patientTranslation: Some hamstring fibers may have been injured. Gentle, gradual strengthening comes before hard running, and return depends on what your sport actually asks your leg to do.
story.clinicianReasoning: Screen suspected proximal avulsion, neural symptoms and severe injury. Progress symptom-guided isometrics to lengthened-strength work, then eccentrics, progressive running speed and full sport exposure with response monitoring.
story.rehabBridge: Low-load contractions → strength at increasing muscle lengths → eccentrics and graded sprinting → sport-specific acceleration and braking.
story.question: A footballer can jog pain-free after hamstring strain but has not done high-speed running. Best return-to-sport decision?
options: Progress to graded high-speed exposure and objective functional criteria
Avoid strengthening and only stretch daily
story.explanation: Return-to-sport decisions require strength, symptom response and actual high-speed demands; pain-free jogging alone is insufficient.
